content: Klebsiella infections are predominantly associated with the bacterium Klebsiella pneumoniae. This organism is a known cause of bacterial pneumonia, which often arises due to aspiration, particularly in individuals with alcoholism. However, K. pneumoniae is more frequently implicated in hospital-acquired infections, such as urinary tract infections (UTIs) and wound infections, especially in immunocompromised patients. Patients suffering from Klebsiella pneumoniae-induced pneumonia often produce a distinctive sputum that resembles red-currant jelly. Among older adults, Klebsiella ranks second only to Escherichia coli as a cause of urinary tract infections. Additionally, it acts as an opportunistic pathogen in individuals with chronic pulmonary diseases, enteric pathogenicity, nasal mucosa atrophy, and rhinoscleroma. The primary source of Klebsiella infections is fecal contamination, followed by contact with contaminated medical instruments. Members of the Klebsiella genus typically express two types of antigens on their cell surface. The first is the O antigen, a lipopolysaccharide with nine known varieties. The second is the K antigen, a capsular polysaccharide with over 80 identified varieties. Both antigens contribute to the bacterium's pathogenicity and are used for subtyping. Research conducted at King’s College London has suggested that molecular mimicry between HLA-B27 and two molecules found in Klebsiella microbes may play a role in the development of ankylosing spondylitis. In general, Klebsiella infections are more likely to occur in individuals with weakened immune systems, often due to poor nutrition. Many of these infections are acquired during hospital stays for unrelated medical conditions. Outside of hospital settings, pneumonia is the most common infection caused by Klebsiella bacteria. This form of pneumonia tends to affect individuals with underlying conditions such as alcoholism, diabetes, or chronic lung disease. Klebsiella bacteria possess a chromosomal class A beta-lactamase enzyme, which confers resistance to ampicillin. Many strains have also acquired extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), granting additional resistance to antibiotics such as carbenicillin, amoxicillin, beta-lactamase inhibitors, and increasingly to ceftazidime. However, these bacteria remain largely susceptible to aminoglycosides and cephalosporins. The beta-lactamase enzyme can be variably inhibited by clavulanic acid. The emergence of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens in intensive care units (ICUs) has led to the renewed use of colistin, an antibiotic that had fallen out of favor for decades. Unfortunately, colistin-resistant strains of Klebsiella pneumoniae have been reported in Greek ICUs. Community-acquired pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae is sometimes referred to as Friedländer’s Pneumonia, named after Carl Friedländer.
